title: The Kingdom of Kongo
hookLine: Afonso I of Kongo, a devout Catholic king who wrote to Portugal to protest the slave traders
tomorrow: The slave trade and the Church

cards: What does a king do when the Christian kingdom that sent him priests is also carrying off his people? This one writes.
His letters, in Portuguese, go by ship from central Africa to the king of Portugal, whom he calls his brother. He asks for priests, teachers, medicine, books. Then the tone changes.
Traders from Portugal, he writes, are seizing his people, free people, even his own nobles and relatives, and shipping them away. He asks his brother king to stop it.
The writer is a baptized Catholic, a ruler who built churches in his capital and prayed in them. His name is Afonso, king of Kongo.

teach.b: The Kingdom of Kongo sat along the great river that still carries its name. First, a faith chosen. When Portuguese ships arrived, Kongo's king and court were baptized.
Afonso, born Mvemba a Nzinga, became a Christian and studied the faith with the priests. Kongo was not conquered into the Church; its own rulers brought the faith in. Second, a Catholic court.

teach.h: CHURCHES AND SCHOOLS AT SÃO SALVADOR.
teach.b: As king, Afonso built churches in his capital, which came to be called São Salvador, Holy Savior. He set up schools and sent young Kongolese, among them his own son Henrique, to study in Portugal.
Henrique was ordained, and later made a bishop.
Third, the letters. They survive, and they are not polite paperwork.
He tells Portugal's king that merchants are carrying off his subjects and emptying his land, and asks that only priests and teachers be sent, not traders. Fourth, the cost.
Kongo itself held captives and sold some, and in time Afonso settled for officials who checked whether each person sold had been lawfully enslaved.

teach.h: THE TRADE GOES ON, THE FAITH TOO.
teach.b: The trade did not stop. Neither did Kongo's faith: for generations, Kongolese Catholics kept churches, feasts and lay leaders of their own, often with very few priests.
At the end of Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sends the apostles out: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations."
In Kongo, the nation was teaching too: an African king reminding a European one that he had asked for teachers, not traders.

how: Catholics in Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo remember the old Kingdom of Kongo, and the ruins of the old cathedral at Mbanza Kongo are visited as a sign of that early Church.

practice: Remember Afonso, a believer asking his own Church to do right. Then bring to mind one person you know, or know of, with roots in Africa, and what they carry: a language, a song, a way of praying.
If you pray, pray for the Church in Africa and the descendants of Kongo; if you don't, let your good wishes go out to them.
